Article Title: 'BJP like Angad's foot': Amit Shah warns Akhilesh, says SP won't return to power in UP for 30 years
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Union home minister Amit Shah on Friday sharpened his attack against the Samajwadi Party and said that it would remain out of power in Uttar Pradesh for the next 30 years.Addressing the Bharatiya Janata Party's state working committee meeting in Lucknow, Shah said that while the SP ordered firing on Ram devotees, the BJP built the Ram temple in Ayodhya."I want to ask them, on what grounds do they talk about forming a government? They ordered firing on Ram devotees, while we have built the Ram temple," he said, referring to the events of October 30, 1990, when police opened fire on kar sevaks in Ayodhya.“Akhilesh Babu, mark my words, your party will not form the government in Uttar Pradesh for the next 30 years. The people will not forgive even your third generation," he added.The home minister also said that the BJP in Uttar Pradesh could not be dislodged as the government had firmly established itself in the state."The BJP government in Uttar Pradesh is like Angad's foot. Nobody can move it. The BJP is going to form the government again. There should be no doubt about it," he said.Moreover, Shah also declared that if the BJP forms the government in Uttar Pradesh for a third time, the UCC will be implemented in the state."This time, when the government comes to power, UCC will be implemented in Uttar Pradesh. UCC has already been implemented in many states," he said.Shah also attacked opposition parties over their allegations of vote theft and compared their complaints to a team blaming the umpire after losing a match."After losing the match, they are blaming the umpire and alleging vote theft. The BJP is ready for a discussion in Parliament. Let them come today and convene a special session. We are ready to answer every question. Let there be a discussion in Parliament," he said.This comes as the BJP's state working committee meeting was held at the Dr Ram Manohar Lohia National Law University auditorium. The meeting was chaired by BJP state president and Union minister of state for finance Pankaj Chaudhary.Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath , deputy chief ministers Keshav Prasad Maurya and Brajesh Pathak, BJP state in-charge Vinod Tawde and national general secretary Smriti Irani were among those present.
Article Summary: Union home minister Amit Shah sharpened his attack against the Samajwadi Party. He said that while the SP ordered firing on Ram devotees, the BJP built the Ram temple. Shah also declared that if the BJP forms the government in Uttar Pradesh for a third time, the UCC will be implemented in the state.

NEW DELHI: A helicopter with six people onboard crashed near Joshimath in Uttarakhand’s Chamoli district while travelling from Badrinath to Dehradun. One pilot and five passengers were on board the chopper.The helicopter, reportedly operated by Charlie X-ray Company, was reported missing near Hathi Parvat, prompting authorities to deploy two other choppers to locate it.Police, SDRF, Army and ITBP personnel have been dispatched to the site for relief and rescue operations, officials told PTI."At 14.21hrs, information was received from the SDM Joshimath regarding the crash landing of a helicopter above Chai village in the Joshimath area. In this regard, UCADA officials stated that the location of a Trans Bharat helicopter, which was flying from Badrinath to Sahastradhara, is showing near the Army Camp above Chai village," Sub-Inspector Manohar Kanyal, Joshimath Post told news agency ANI.Uttarakhand CM Pushkar Singh Dhami said the aircraft crashed near Chayee village, close to Joshimath, and that a joint rescue operation was underway involving the district administration, disaster management department and State Disaster Response Force (SDRF).“We have received the unfortunate news of a helicopter crash near Chayee village, close to Joshimath. A joint rescue operation is being conducted by the district administration, disaster management department, and SDRF,” Dhami wrote in a post on X.He added that he was personally monitoring the situation and that instructions had been issued to airlift the seriously injured to advanced medical facilities for treatment.
Article Summary: A helicopter with six people onboard crashed near Joshimath in Uttarakhand’s Chamoli district. One pilot and five passengers were on board the chopper. The helicopter was reported missing near Hathi Parvat, prompting authorities to deploy two other choppers to locate it.

Article Title: 'Will serve until my last breath': PM Modi declares in Gujarat - top quotes
Article Text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi addresses the inauguration and foundation stone laying of various developmental projects, in Banaskantha district, Gujarat. (NarendraModi/YT)

Here are the key quotes from PM Modi's address:

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday said he would continue serving people until his last breath as he addressed a public event in Gujarat's Banaskantha, where he inaugurated and laid the foundation stone for development projects worth over Rs 14,000 crore.The Prime Minister spoke about his 25 years in public office, the government's support for farmers amid global uncertainties and the use of technology in agriculture and animal husbandry. He also accused some people of spreading rumours about fertiliser and gas shortages to defame the government.1. 'I will continue serving people until my last breath'Referring to his 25 years in public office, PM Modi said, "On October 7, I completed 25 years in public office. But it feels like just yesterday when I first took the oath of office in October 2001; you showered me with a lot of love.""I will continue serving people until my last breath," he said.2. 'Our government did not let fertiliser price rise burden farmers'Addressing concerns over global uncertainties and tensions in the Gulf, Modi said his government had protected farmers from rising international fertiliser prices."Amid global uncertainties, there was a huge jump in the price of fertilisers, but our government, which is dedicated to the welfare of farmers, did not let the burden of this price rise fall on farmers. The government spent Rs 16 lakh crore on this..."3. 'Some people feel happy when the country faces difficulty'The Prime Minister accused some people of spreading rumours about shortages of fertilisers and gas amid tensions in the Gulf."Today, every youth, sister and daughter is working towards making India a developed nation. But some people do not like this. These are the people who want to see the country in difficulty. They feel happy when they see the country in difficulty. When the nation as one is facing uncertainties emerging due to tensions in the Gulf, they spread rumours about shortages of fertilisers and gas. They wanted to do this only to defame Modi. I want to remind the farmers and all others that I had said that I would stand by you all. The tensions in the Gulf are still ongoing, but the govt did not let the burden of increased fertiliser prices across the world fall on our farmers..."4. 'Our government has always prioritised farmers' welfare'Modi said his government had focused on supporting farmers and empowering them through various initiatives. He said Rs 4.5 lakh crore had been transferred to small farmers under the PM-Kisan Samman Nidhi scheme.5. 'Agriculture is our culture'Speaking about the use of technology in agriculture, Modi said the government had connected farming and animal husbandry with technological advancements."Agriculture is our culture. We connected farming and animal husbandry with technology. More than 26 crore soil health cards have been availed by farmers today," he said.6. 'Animal husbandry is an important part of our rural economy'The Prime Minister also spoke about the contribution of women to the animal husbandry and dairy sectors."Animal husbandry is an important part of our rural economy. Our sisters have a very significant participation in it. In the past decade, we have emphasised the use of science and technology in the animal husbandry and dairy sectors as well," he said.During his visit to the Bharat Bovine Breeding and Research Centre (BBBRC) cattle farm at Bhildi, a group of women chanted, "Modi will not leave" while posing for a photograph with the Prime Minister.The 127-acre facility has been established as a Centre of Excellence to strengthen bovine breeding, genetic upgradation and advanced reproductive technologies. It is the country's first facility dedicated to the Kankrej cattle breed and is expected to accelerate breed improvement by 10-20 times.Gujarat chief minister Bhupendra Patel and Deputy Chief Minister Harsh Sanghavi were also present at the event.
Article Summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressed a public event in Gujarat's Banaskantha. He laid the foundation stone for development projects worth over Rs 14,000 crore. Modi spoke about his 25 years in public office, the government's support for farmers amid global uncertainties and the use of technology in agriculture.

NEW DELHI: Politcal barbs were exchanged on Friday as Prime Minister Narendra Modi interacted with a group of students during his visit to the Bharat Bovine Breeding and Research Centre (BBBRC) cattle farm in Gujarat’s Banaskantha district on Friday, when chants of “Modi nahi jayenge” was heard. In response, Congress responded with "you wish".The slogan, which translates to “Modi will not leave”, was raised as the Prime Minister posed for a group photograph and interacted with those present at the cattle farm.To this, Congress leader Pawan Khera took a jab saying, "You wish!" "Hey, for now, the boss won't even go to Parliament. Let the Parliament session start, and you'll see a mad rush to flee the country and the world!" he added.This comes days after Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge sparked controversy with his “Modi ka baap bhi jayega” remark after a member of the audience interjected during his speech at a Patna event to say that “the PM would not go anywhere” . PM Modi visited the Centre at Bhildi, a 127-acre facility focused on improving the breeding and genetics of the Kankrej cattle breed. The Centre of Excellence is equipped to promote advanced reproductive technologies, with breed improvement expected to accelerate by 10–20 times.Gujarat chief minister Bhupendra Patel and deputy chief minister Harsh Sanghavi were also present.The visit was part of a wider programme in which PM Modi inaugurated and laid the foundation stones for development projects worth over Rs 14,000 crore in the state. He also released the 24th instalment of PM-KISAN, amounting to Rs 19,000 crore.Ahmedabad’s metro network is set for expansion under two projects covering the airport and GIFT City. Phase-2A will connect Koteshwar Road to the airport through five stations across more than 6 km, while Phase-2B will link GIFT City and Shahpur through three stations across 3.3 km.Another major transport project involves widening the Ahmedabad-Mehsana Road (State Highway-41) from four lanes to eight. Estimated to cost around Rs 2,600 crore, the upgrade is expected to improve connectivity between Ahmedabad and North Gujarat.The state’s dairy sector is also set to get two Bio-CNG plants operated by Banas Dairy at Tharad and Radhanpur. The facilities will process 75 metric tonnes and 100 metric tonnes of cattle dung per day, respectively.In childcare infrastructure, 4,030 new child-friendly Anganwadi centres are planned, while 361 completed centres will be inaugurated. The Rs 800-crore initiative is expected to benefit more than four lakh people.PM Modi will also dedicate 521 projects developed under the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund to the nation. Costing around Rs 4,950 crore collectively, the projects include cold storage facilities, warehouses, silos, greenhouses and integrated processing units.Other initiatives include an expanded potato processing plant at Sanadar and an automated storage and retrieval system for ultra-high-temperature products at Palanpur.
Article Summary: PM Narendra Modi visited Bhildi, a 127-acre facility focused on improving the breeding and genetics of the Kankrej cattle breed. Part of a wider programme in which PM Modi inaugurated and laid the foundation stones for development projects worth over Rs 14,000 crore.

Article Title: Night polo goesmainstream in Jaipur
Article Text:
A night polo match underway at the Rambagh Polo Club ground in Jaipur

An Evening At The Polo

In this bastion of the ‘sport of kings’, horse and rider are routinely taking to the field under floodlights, in the hope of drawing a wider audience, building tourism opportunities — and preserving a bit of the city’s heritage, writes Mandakini Shaly

A Place In The City

Finding Players And Spectators

Later Dinners For The Horses

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Polo in Jaipur has become easier to catch. Matches at the Rambagh Polo Club ground now begin at 7.30pm, giving office-goers time to get there after work and families a chance to watch once the daytime heat has passed.Over the past couple of months, 10 newly installed floodlights have lit up the ground near the Vidhan Sabha and the high court. In a neighbourhood where lights over the Sawai Man Singh Stadium have long signalled IPL season, there is now another reason to stop for a match.The stands have young spectators watching their first game, taking selfies and discovering a sport whose familiar audience has largely been drawn from royal families, the cavalry and club circles. Broad-brimmed hats, pastel linen jackets and chiffon sarees are still in evidence. The club is hoping to give more people a reason to come.Night polo has been played in Hyderabad and Noida, in smaller arenas with sand surfaces. Jaipur’s matches are on a full-sized grass ground, under lights, as part of the official tournament schedule.For Major Anant Rajpurohit of 61 Cavalry, a veteran player, the advantage is straightforward: more people are free to watch.“The good point is that people tend to get off from work, office, or day commitments, and the attendance is more,” he says.“Earlier, the matches and all the finals were done during the daytime, so the availability of gentlemen and ladies was very restricted and very confined. The development of any sport comes when the number of people watching it is more. Then, the number of people who intend to get into the sport or invest into the sport increases. So that way it is an added advantage,” he says.For Padmanabh Singh, 28, India’s polo captain and scion of the erstwhile Jaipur royal family, encouraging people to watch is also part of keeping a city tradition alive.“I have always viewed polo as very intertwined with the culture of Jaipur,” he says. “Jaipur is one of the main hubs of polo across the world and has given a lot to the sport. Some of the most iconic moments have happened here. So when I talk about conservation, restoration, and preservation of our culture and heritage, I mean polo too. It’s part of our tourism.”Rambagh Polo Club is marketing the sport more actively, with support from Rajasthan’s tourism leadership. Padmanabh’s mother, Diya Kumari, is deputy chief minister and tourism minister.Last month, a UAE delegation visited Jaipur to discuss cooperation in polo, horses and tourism. Among its interests was the Marwari, Rajasthan’s indigenous horse breed.“The Marwari is our local breed here in Rajasthan, and the visiting delegation was incredibly keen to see them. We discussed avenues to encourage a vibrant cultural exchange between the UAE, Rajasthan Tourism, and Rambagh Polo Club. They are very eager to support polo further and bring global visibility to this magnificent breed that has served Rajasthan for centuries,” Padmanabh says.Elsewhere, access to a convenient ground is a concern. Delhi, Maharashtra and West Bengal have active polo circuits, supported by the Army, professional players and corporate patrons. In Delhi, however, Rajpurohit worries that a change of venue will cost the sport spectators and sponsors.“The finals of all elite tournaments in Delhi used to be at Jaipur Polo Ground, which is in the heart of Delhi,” he says. “Unfortunately, we lost that ground a few months back. Now more matches will be conducted at the Army Polo and Riding Centre. It is a shame that we lost the ground in the heart of Delhi. The number of people who used to attend and sponsor the events were more. Now that number will reduce.”He sees encouraging signs in the number of younger players taking up the sport.“The number of horses that have been shipped in every year is increasing. The number of kids who intend to compete in the sport is increasing. Earlier we used to have around four odd teams in Junior National Championship. Now we have six-seven teams,” he adds.Polo remains expensive to take up, though schools are helping introduce children to it.“There are many schools that are offering the equestrian part and the polo part, like Mayo and Delhi College, and they are coming up very well.”In Jaipur, demand for lessons already exceeds what the Sawai Man Singh Polo School and Academy can offer.“With that spirit in mind, a few years ago we started the Sawai Man Singh Polo School and Academy. It’s the only one of its kind and it’s doing very well. We have 50 students, which is our maximum capacity, and for the last three years, we have had a waiting list,” Padmanabh says.“Unfortunately, we can’t accommodate more because we have a limited number of horses, but it’s in the heart of the city and subsidised by the polo club. I donated some of my horses to the academy and I go there all the time to mentor them. Whenever someone is doing well, I pull them out to play with us,” Padmanabh says.Padmanabh says Jaipur’s experience of playing after dark goes back more than a century. He describes a brass night polo ball, with a small candle inside, used by women who played at night.At Rambagh, playing under floodlights requires a change in the horses’ routine. Matches fall at what would ordinarily be their dinner time.“I would not say that it changes much. We just have to adjust the feeding time. Now, they have to have dinner a little bit later. So we just have to adapt our schedules,” Padmanabh says.The horses, he says, have settled into the later hours without trouble.“We know that if the horse is not happy, it won’t eat, or it will stop drinking water, or it will stop laying down. None of that happens. In fact, it is better for them because they don’t have the heat of the day.”
Article Summary: Polo in Jaipur has become easier to catch. Matches at the Rambagh Polo Club ground now begin at 7.30pm. 10 newly installed floodlights have lit up the ground near the Vidhan Sabha. Padmanabh Singh, 28, India’s polo captain, says it is part of a city tradition.

NEW DELHI: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Friday defended the Centre's proposed sale of a controlling stake in IDBI Bank , hitting back at Congress leader Rahul Gandhi 's criticism and accusing previous Congress-led governments of political interference and financial mismanagement.Responding to Rahul's opposition to the proposed sale of the bank to a subsidiary of Canada's Fairfax Financial Holdings, Sitharaman said IDBI Bank was in a "distressed state when the NDA government took charge."In a post on X, the finance minister said previous Congress-led governments had treated banks and financial institutions as personal entities, pressuring employees to extend loans by bypassing lending norms."We all know how Congress has used Banks and financial institutions as personal entities and pressured bank employees to extend loans at their whim, bypassing prudent lending norms. Let me list a few instances. - In 1957, Haridas Mundra got money from LIC due to influence by the Congress leaders. - In 1976, Indira Gandhi's government removed SBI Chairman R.K. Talwar after he refused political pressure to relax lending conditions for a company linked to Sanjay Gandhi's circle.- Sanjay Gandhi pressured the Central Bank of India over loans to Maruti. - B. Janardhana Poojary, MoS Finance under Indira Gandhi and Rajiv Gandhi — pressured bank employees to issue loans in the 1980s. - Pawan Kumar Bansal, as a minister in the UPA, pressured Canara Bank to give loans to his family-linked businesses," she posted.Sitharaman also accused previous administrations of pushing IDBI bank to extend loans to large business groups with alleged links to Congress leaders. She named Videocon, Winsome, ABG Shipyard and Kingfisher, saying the loans later turned into non-performing assets (NPAs) and caused huge losses to the lender."The IDBI Bank was handed over to us in poor shape, as IDBI itself was forced to lend to large business groups with close connections to @INCIndia leaders such as Videocon, Winsome, ABG Shipyard, Kingfisher, etc. These turned into bad loans, causing huge losses for IDBI Bank, which we recognised," she added.The finance minister also cited a series of historical controversies to support her argument, including the 1957 Mundra scandal, the removal of State Bank of India chairman RK Talwar in 1976, alleged pressure over loans to Maruti and instances of political interference during the 1980s and the UPA era.Earlier on Friday, Rahul Gandhi extended support to IDBI Bank employees amid protests by bank unions and political parties against the Centre's decision to sell its stake in the lender.In a post on X, the Congress leader shared a letter addressed to the IDBI Bank family, criticising the government's move and contrasting it with the bank's establishment during the Congress regime."During Congress's time, IDBI was established—to build the nation's industry. During Modi's time, first the bidding was seen, then the price was set," he said."During Congress's time, banks were being created. During Modi's time, they are being sold. I stand with the employees of IDBI Bank," Rahul added.The Centre had said a day earlier that the proposed stake sale was part of a "strategic restructuring". It maintained that the process followed the provisions laid down in the request for proposal (RFP) and was undertaken after approval from a panel of secretaries and the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs.The latest exchange marks the second round of sharp exchanges between Rahul and Sitharaman in three days. The two had first traded barbs on Wednesday over the boardroom battle at Bombay House, with Rahul accusing the government of allowing the Tata Group to be "criminally destroyed".Rahul had taken to X to criticise the developments at the conglomerate, saying, “Tata is being criminally destroyed, and no business leader dares say a word. How long will you stay silent? Until they own you? Indian business is not Modi and Shah’s plaything. You lack courage. We don’t. We will ensure justice for these crimes,”Within hours, Sitharaman hit back at the Congress leader, saying, “Being the LoP (leader of opposition in Lok Sabha) Rahul Gandhi, I suggest you refrain from politicising every issue. Also, casually labelling commercial and legal matters as criminal is unacceptable,”She also accused the Congress of harming the interests of Indian business.
Article Summary: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman hits back at Congress leader Rahul Gandhi's criticism. She accuses previous Congress-led governments of political interference and financial mismanagement. Earlier on Friday, Rahul Gandhi extended support to IDBI Bank employees amid protests by bank unions.

Article Title: '20 markets, Rs 12,000cr trade at stake': Delhi traders urge Sonia Gandhi to defer Rahul Gandhi's November 1 rally
Article Text:
Delhi traders flag parking, traffic concerns; urge Sonia Gandhi to defer Rahul's rally

Parking and traffic concerns

NEW DELHI: The Chamber of Trade and Industry (CTI) in Delhi on Friday urged senior Congress leader Sonia Gandhi to postpone the party's proposed mega rally at Ramlila Maidan on November 1, warning that it could disrupt business worth Rs 10,000-12,000 crore across 20 markets in the national capital.The trade body said the rally, proposed by leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi, comes at a crucial time when markets are preparing for the Diwali shopping season.The trade body warned of severe economic losses during the peak festive shopping season.The Chamber of Trade and Industry (CTI) said the rally is expected to draw around 10 lakh people and 15,000 to 20,000 vehicles to central Delhi. It warned that the large gathering could lead to severe traffic congestion and affect the movement of goods and shoppers across the markets."We demand to reschedule the mega-rally of 1 million (10 lakh) people, planned for November 1, to a date after Diwali; lack of parking for 15,000–20,000 vehicles could lead to a total gridlock, akin to a lockdown," the CTI urged in its letter to Sonia Gandhi.The traders' body said the rally is planned at a crucial time for businesses, with Dhanteras falling on November 6 and Diwali on November 8. It said November 1 is expected to be one of the busiest days for transporting festive goods and for shoppers visiting the markets.CTI chairman Brijesh Goyal said traders were worried about the possible impact on their livelihoods and stressed that the appeal was not against the rally."We are not opposing the rally; we are making a heartfelt plea to protect our livelihoods during the peak Diwali season," stated CTI Chairman Brijesh Goyal."These 20 markets are not merely marketplaces; they are the heartbeat of Delhi. They generate a daily turnover of 10,000 to 12,000 crore rupees, and Dhanteras falls on November 6th. Traders are anxious: if a lockdown-like gridlock hits central Delhi on October 31st and November 1st, how will the goods for Dhanteras be transported in and out?" Goyal added."Dhanteras falls on November 6, and Diwali is on November 8; November 1 is the busiest day for preparations... If 1 million people and 15,000–20,000 vehicles arrive in Central Delhi on November 1, the daily business turnover of Rs 10,000–12,000 crore across 20 historic markets will come to a complete standstill," Goyal noted.In its letter, the CTI listed four major concerns. The first was the lack of parking space at Ramlila Maidan."Where will 15,000–20,000 vehicles be parked? Ramlila Maidan does not even have the capacity to park 200 large buses."The second concern was the possible disruption to 20 wholesale and retail markets within a 5-km radius of the venue. The CTI said these markets together record daily business worth Rs 10,000-12,000 crore.The markets include Chandni Chowk, Sadar Bazar, Connaught Place, Palika Bazar, Janpath, Bhagirath Palace, Khari Baoli, Kashmiri Gate, Naya Bazar, Lajpat Rai Market, Chawri Bazar, Kinari Bazar, Dariba Kalan, Ballimaran, Fatehpuri, Tilak Bazar, Karol Bagh, Jama Masjid, Nabi Karim, Gaffar Market, Ajmeri Gate-Paharganj and Daryaganj.The traders' body also warned that traffic restrictions could begin well before the rally. It said buses and other vehicles may start arriving at Delhi's borders, including Singhu, Tikri, Ghazipur and Badarpur, from the afternoon of October 31. Barricades could also be put up along Bahadur Shah Zafar Marg and JLN Marg by the evening.The CTI said transporters had already begun refusing to send vehicles to the markets from October 31.It also cited the traffic disruption during an earlier protest as a reason for concern."On October 10th, with only 5,000 to 7,000 people gathering at Jantar Mantar, central Delhi remained gridlocked for eight hours. Now, 1 million (10 lakh) people are expected to arrive."The CTI said the markets, some of which are up to 300 years old, supply goods to different parts of the country. It added that their operations depend on around 5,000 trucks and tempos arriving daily from 56 industrial areas, including Narela, Bawana, Okhla, Mayapuri, Mundka, Udyog Nagar and Mangolpuri.To avoid disruption during the festive season, the CTI has suggested two options. It has asked the organisers to postpone the rally until after November 10 or shift it to Burari Maidan if the November 1 date cannot be changed.The rally, called the 'Chalo Dilli Ramlila March', has been organised by the opposition INDIA bloc to protest against alleged vote tampering.Congress leader Rahul Gandhi has said the march is not limited to any one political party and has appealed to people to join it."Chalo Dilli Ramlila March, it is a march to save democracy, to stop vote theft, to save the Constitution. This is not a march of any one political party; it is a march of the soul of India. All the people who are fed up with Narendra Modi, Amit Shah, and Gyanesh Kumar, all the people who want to save democracy, who want to protect the Constitution, you all come," Rahul Gandhi stated.The letter to Sonia Gandhi came after the trade body had also written to Rahul Gandhi, urging him to postpone the rally to avoid disrupting business during the festive season.With less than 48 hours left before the rally, traders are waiting for a response from the Congress leadership to their request.
Article Summary: Chamber of Trade and Industry (CTI) urges Sonia Gandhi to postpone Rahul Gandhi's rally. The rally is expected to draw around 10 lakh people and 15,000 to 20,000 vehicles to central Delhi. It warned that the large gathering could lead to severe traffic congestion and affect the movement of goods and shoppers.

Article Title: Firecracker ban: No point in passing orders without enforcement, says SC

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Thursday said it was not inclined to completely ban firecrackers, but there was no point in passing orders and directions every year unless authorities implement them on the ground.“It concerns every living being,” a bench of Justices M M Sundresh and Prasanna B Varale observed while hearing a matter on the bursting of firecrackers in Delhi-NCR.Additional solicitor-general Aishwarya Bhati told the bench about the measures taken by Delhi govt and Commission for Air Quality Management to deal with air pollution.“There is no point in passing orders and directions unless you give effect to them on the ground, otherwise, it becomes a mockery,” the bench observed, while stressing enforcement.While saying that it was not an adversarial matter, the bench observed that authorities have to take up the issue seriously and take action. “You have to really regulate it. Every year we are trying to balance it out but unless there is cooperation from everyone, it can’t be done,” it said.“We also understand the sentiments of the public. We are not inclined to completely ban, but don’t push us to take a very harsh stand,” the bench told Bhati.Bhati said a series of measures have been taken which would come into effect from Nov, including curbs on older vehicles, construction and demolition activity and staggered office timings in Delhi. “We are geared up to deal with the pollution season which unfortunately happens,” she said.Centre also told the bench that its internal consultation on the issue pertaining to the use of barium in firecrackers was going on. Bhati requested the bench to grant three weeks to complete the consultation.The top court was hearing two petitions, including a suo motu case concerning air pollution in NCR covering issues like firecrackers, stubble burning and solid waste management. The other plea relates to a ban on manufacturing firecrackers.During the hearing, an advocate, assisting the apex court as an amicus curiae in the suo motu case, said bursting firecrackers releases a huge amount of hazardous particulate matter (PM) which enters the human body and causes damage to lungs and other organs.She said during Dussehra last week, there was a spike in the Air Quality Index (AQI) in Delhi-NCR. Flagging the issue of enforcement, the amicus said there was no proper mechanism to assess whether the firecrackers which are being sold are actually green crackers.The bench had said that a middle ground would have to be found by specifying hours during which firecrackers could be used.
Article Summary: SC said it is not inclined to completely ban firecrackers but warned authorities that orders are meaningless without ground-level enforcement. “There is no point in passing orders and directions unless you give effect to them on the ground, otherwise, it becomes a mockery,” the bench observed, while stressing enforcement.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Friday cancelled the bail granted to expelled JD(U) MLA Anant Singh in the murder case of Dularchand Yadav and directed him to surrender before the authorities on or before December 1, 2026.A bench of Justices MM Sundresh and PV Varale observed that the Patna High Court had erred in granting Singh bail without adequately considering the nature of the offence and his criminal antecedents. Article Title: MLC election results: BJP wins big, but Congress and Samajwadi Party send a message from Nagpur, Varanasi
Article Text:
BJP's big win in MLC elections comes with setbacks in Nagpur and Varanasi

BJP-led NDA secured 16 of the 28 MLC seats across four states, while the SP won five seats in Uttar Pradesh and Congress retained Nagpur in Maharashtra.

BJP mocks Congress over 'zero' seats

BJP president Nitin Nabin targeted Congress over its poor performance in the MLC elections, pointing out that voting had taken place using ballot papers.

Nagpur win gives Congress a chance to respond

Congress leader Jairam Ramesh questioned the BJP's setbacks in Nagpur and Varanasi after PM Modi mocked the party's performance in the MLC elections.

Varanasi setback gives SP a boost ahead of 2027

What do the results mean for 2027?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The MLC elections across four states brought both shock and cheer for the BJP and Congress. While the Congress suffered a humiliating defeat in Karnataka, where it is in power but failed to win a single seat, the BJP faltered in two constituencies which mattered the most. One being Nagpur, which is home to the RSS headquarters, and Varanasi, Prime Minister Narendra Modi's parliamentary constituency.The BJP nevertheless emerged as the largest party, winning 13 of the 28 seats contested, while its allies took the NDA's tally to 16. The alliance swept all four seats in Karnataka, won six of the 11 seats in Uttar Pradesh and secured four of the eight seats in Bihar. In Maharashtra, the ruling Mahayuti won two of the five seats, while the opposition Maha Vikas Aghadi secured three.The Congress's only victory came from Nagpur, a political stronghold of Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis and Union minister Nitin Gadkari. In Uttar Pradesh, the Samajwadi Party retained the Varanasi Teachers' constituency and was heading towards victory in the Graduates' seat, both of which it had won in 2020.What began as celebrations and sharp jibes at the Congress on Wednesday turned into a war of words on Thursday, as the results in Nagpur and Varanasi gave the opposition grounds to question the BJP's claims of electoral dominance.As the early results came in on Wednesday, BJP leaders targeted the Congress over its poor performance, particularly in Karnataka, where the party is in power but failed to win a single seat.PM Modi took a swipe at the opposition party on X, pointing out that voting in the four states had taken place using ballot papers."Guess how many seats Congress won?" he asked.The remark came amid the Congress's repeated allegations over electronic voting machines and its demand for a return to ballot-paper voting.BJP president Nitin Nabin also targeted the Congress, saying the party had failed to win public support despite voting being conducted using ballot papers."The people are repeatedly rejecting Congress' anarchist politics," Nabin said, adding that public trust remained with PM Modi irrespective of whether elections were conducted using EVMs or ballot papers.BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi also attacked Rahul Gandhi over his allegations of vote theft"Kamchori ki aadat chhodiye. Vote chori ka shabd apke muh se khud chhoot jayega," he said, asking the Congress leader to give up what he described as a habit of avoiding hard work.Congress candidate and sitting MLC Abhijeet Wanjari defeated BJP's Sudhakar Kohale to retain the Nagpur Division Graduates' constituency after more than 40 hours of counting.Kohale had initially taken the lead before Wanjari overtook him through preferential votes.Nagpur is important for the BJP. Besides housing the RSS headquarters, it is associated with Fadnavis and Gadkari, both of whom campaigned for Kohale.The Congress had wrested the seat from the BJP in 2020, when Wanjari defeated Sandip Joshi. By retaining it in 2026, the party prevented the BJP from reclaiming a constituency it had dominated for decades.The Maharashtra Congress also targeted Fadnavis over a social media post in which he had claimed that the party had failed to win a single seat.Sharing a screenshot of what it said was a deleted post by Fadnavis, the party accused him of celebrating before counting was complete. The post had described the Congress's performance as a "big fat zero".The Congress said Fadnavis had been forced to delete the post after the Nagpur result and warned that the outcome was only a trailer of future political battles.Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh also responded to PM Modi's remarks, questioning the BJP's losses in Nagpur and Varanasi."The Prime Minister needs to introspect, but instead, he's lecturing others! Before counting Congress's seats, I wish he'd also reflect on why the BJP lost both seats in his own parliamentary constituency of Varanasi, and how Congress managed to defeat the BJP in RSS's stronghold of Nagpur?" Ramesh said."Mr. Modi, stop the trolling," he added, accusing the government of failing to address inflation, unemployment and weak private investment.Ramesh claimed that voters in Varanasi, Nagpur, Lucknow, Prayagraj and Patna had expressed dissatisfaction with the Centre's policies.The BJP's biggest setback in Uttar Pradesh came from Varanasi, where the Samajwadi Party retained the Teachers' seat and established an unassailable lead in the Graduates' constituency.The BJP retained six of the 11 seats contested in the state, while the SP won four and was heading towards a fifth.The SP had won both Varanasi seats in 2020 as well. Six years later, the BJP has failed to dislodge the party from either constituency despite its strong presence in the region.Although the two MLC constituencies cover a wider geographical area than PM Modi's Lok Sabha seat, the results carry political significance given Varanasi's association with the Prime Minister since 2014.They also come after PM Modi's victory margin in Varanasi declined from nearly 4.8 lakh votes in the 2019 Lok Sabha elections to around 1.5 lakh in 2024.Across Uttar Pradesh, the SP's tally is set to rise from three seats in 2020 to five, while the BJP has retained its tally of six.The SP had also emerged as the largest party in Uttar Pradesh in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, winning 37 of the state's 80 parliamentary seats against the BJP's 33.BJP deputy chief minister Keshav Prasad Maurya acknowledged that the party had expected a better performance."These elections are decided by highly educated and qualified voters. The BJP has repeated its previous performance, but we expected to win more seats. We will examine why we fell short," Maurya said.The SP, meanwhile, has repeatedly accused the BJP of electoral irregularities, allegations the ruling party has rejected.On polling day, Akhilesh Yadav had claimed that the BJP was attempting to influence even the MLC elections, which have a limited electorate."If the BJP can do this in MLC polls for teachers and graduate constituencies where a limited number of people cast votes, one can imagine their preparation for the assembly polls," he had said.The NDA's overall tally shows that the BJP and its allies remain ahead in these Legislative Council contests. But the results in Nagpur and Varanasi also show that the party has struggled to regain certain seats despite its strong presence in both regions.In Uttar Pradesh, the SP and Congress are preparing to contest the 2027 assembly elections together, hoping to build on their performance in the 2024 Lok Sabha polls.The alliance won 43 of the state's 80 parliamentary seats in 2024, reducing the BJP's tally from 62 in 2019 to 33. Akhilesh Yadav has said the alliance will continue in 2027, although the two parties still need to settle their seat-sharing arrangement.The MLC results, however, cannot be treated as an indication of how the state will vote in the assembly elections. These contests involve a limited electorate of registered graduates and teachers, unlike assembly polls, which are decided by a much wider voter base.For the BJP, which is seeking a third consecutive term in Uttar Pradesh, the challenge will be to counter the opposition's gains. For the SP-Congress alliance, the question is whether it can repeat its 2024 Lok Sabha performance when the state's 403 assembly seats go to the polls in 2027.
Article Summary: BJP-led NDA secured 16 of the 28 MLC seats across four states, while the SP won five seats in Uttar Pradesh and Congress retained Nagpur in Maharashtra. PM Modi mocked Congress over its poor performance, pointing out that voting had taken place using ballot papers.

Article Title: Bihar Museum in world top 10, ahead of Met, Louvre

Artist Subodh Gupta helped put Bihar on the global art map with his signature bartan sculptures.Even so, the art world was surprised to see the barely decade-old Bihar Museum ranked ninth on the 'World's 100 Best Museums 2026' list, ahead of institutions such as New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Louvre in Paris.Published by Munich-based travel publication Worth a Journey, the list ranks the Patna institution as No. 1 in Asia.It is the only Indian museum in the top 100. The rankings draw on visitor reviews, data analytics and on-site expert evaluations.The museum may not have the Mona Lisa, but it has a crown jewel of its own: the Didarganj Yakshi.Carved from a single block of highly polished Chunar sandstone, the 2,000-year-old, life-sized statue stands in an air-conditioned room. Her nose is chipped and her left arm broken, but she seems ready to swat away any obstacle with the fly-whisk (chauri) in her hand.Beyond the Yakshi, the 13.9-acre complex houses the famed Kurkihar bronzes, prehistoric stone tools and a Kushan-period 'Birth of the Buddha' slab. The museum building, designed by Pritzker Prize-winning Japanese architect Fumihiko Maki and Studio Opolis, an architectural practice located in Mumbai and Pune, is quite striking too.On X, industrialist Anand Mahindra called it "a seminal moment of recognition", adding that it has the potential to be a game changer for the museum-going experience in India.

Article Title: Bar bodies foiled plan to rope in ex-judges: Supreme Court

NEW DELHI: With case pendency exceeding 65 lakh in high courts, Supreme Court Thursday lamented that its 2021 judgement for re-engaging retired judges as ad hoc high court judges under Article 224A to speed up case disposal remained on paper, despite having been diluted, because of resistance from bar associations.Dealing with a case related to pension of judges, a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said the attempt to avail services of some retired judges with impeccable integrity to speed up disposal of cases in HCs has not fructified as bar associations are passing resolutions against such appointments.“Retired high court judges have established lucrative practices in Supreme Court or are enjoying better gains in conducting arbitration proceedings or in writing opinions. They are reluctant to become ad hoc judges,” said Justice Bagchi.In 2021, the apex court had activated the dormant Article 224A of Constitution and issued general guidelines for re-engagement of retired judges as ad hoc judges of HCs to help clear backlog of cases, many of them more than 15 years old. In Allahabad HC, there are more than 12 lakh cases pending.On Jan 30 last year, a bench of Justices Sanjiv Khanna, B R Gavai and Surya Kant had diluted certain tough conditions recorded in the 2021 judgment and had said a maximum of five retired HC judges could be reappointed to an HC but their number would not exceed 10% of that HC’s sanctioned judge strength.Two important conditions in the 2021 judgement that were kept in abeyance in Jan 2025 were ad hoc judges can be appointed only when there is less than 20% vacancy in an HC; and if 10% of the pending cases were more than five years old.Till 1970, some retired SC judges were reappointed as ad hoc judges in the apex court. But it was rarely the practice in HCs, with retired judges being appointed only for specific purposes – Justice Suraj Bhan to Madhya Pradesh HC in Nov 1972 for disposal of election petitions; Justice P Venugopal for two years in Madras HC in Aug 1983; and Justice O P Srivastava to Allahabad HC in 2007, as he was part of the special bench hearing Ayodhya suits.
Article Summary: In 2021, the apex court had activated the dormant Article 224A of Constitution. It issued general guidelines for re-engagement of retired judges as ad hoc judges of HCs to help clear backlog of cases. In Allahabad HC, there are more than 12 lakh cases pending.

Article Title: Most of private equity in health went to west & south: Study
Article Text:

A mapping of private equity investments in India’s health sector over past 18 years has revealed investments are overwhelmingly in multispecialty hospitals in the urbanised southern and western states, while vast rural and underserved regions attracted little or no investment at all.In the study by Brown University’s School of Public Health and Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, which identified 70 private equity (PE) backed acquisitions between Jan 2007 and May 2025, over 73% of the investment was in 45 hospital groups, including 187 multispecialty hospitals and several single ones. Among 16 outpatient care providers targeted, ophthalmology and fertility/reproductive care were the most common ones.According to the study, the investments accelerated after 2020 and peaked in 2023, which witnessed 18 deals. “This timing mirrors global post-pandemic trends, where healthcare emerged as an attractive investment sector amid favourable financial conditions. During the pandemic, low interest rates and large amounts of available capital (“dry powder”) made financing inexpensive and widely available, while healthcare’s relatively stable revenues made it more attractive than other economic sectors,” stated the study published in BMC Health Services Research, an open source journal.Karnataka recorded 13 deals, the highest number, followed by 10 each in Maharashtra and Telangana. Gujarat had six deals while Keralam and Haryana saw five each. Northern and eastern states saw minimal or no investment.Four hospital groups that together accounted for one-third of the total deals were Manipal Health Enterprises and Health Care Global Enterprises, both headquartered in Karnataka; and CARE Hospitals and ASG Eye Hospitals.Of the total number of acquisitions, 47 (67.1%) were financed solely by foreign PE firms, including those based in US, Singapore, and Mauritius, while 18 were backed exclusively by Indian investors.Among the 25 observed PE exits, secondary sales to other PE firms were most common (64%) exit strategy. Average holding period among those that exited was 5.1 years, with hospital platforms accounting for over half of these exits.Forty-five hospital groups (64.3%) remained under their original PE ownership.Several of the PE-backed platform deals were initially structured as minority stakes, with ownership expanding gradually over time, a staged pattern of engagement consistent with more cautious, multi-step investment approaches observed elsewhere in Brics markets, noted the study.
Article Summary: Private equity investment in India’s healthcare sector is concentrated in urban hospitals in southern and western states. Rural and underserved regions attracted little or no investment at all. Over 73% of the investment was in 45 hospital groups, including 187 multispecialty hospitals and several single ones.

Article Title: It only takes one rumour: How a small trigger can lead to a deadly stampede
Article Text:
Stampede at Kolkata pandal during Durga Puja claimed 19 lives.

The anatomy of a stampede

Psychology of the crowd

How should police act and react?

Preparing for the unexpected

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: It begins with a rumour, feeds on panic and ends in tragedy. A stampede can turn a celebration into chaos within minutes, leaving thousands gathered in joy struggling to find a way out. In a tightly packed crowd, even a small disturbance can have deadly consequences.A similar script played out in Kolkata on October 17. On the night of Maha Saptami during Durga Puja, pandal-hoppers gathered in large numbers at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin pandal. The crowd swelled further after a sudden spell of rain prompted people waiting outside to seek shelter, while visitors near the exit stopped moving.An announcement over the public address system warning that the pandal was about to collapse added to the panic. Investigators believe several factors contributed to the stampede, including overcrowding, narrow entry and exit points, inadequate crowd management and the misleading announcement.The crowd crush, which police said lasted around three minutes, claimed 19 lives and left at least 25 people injured.India is a country of festivals, and its massive religious gatherings also make it prone to stampedes. This year, it was Kolkata.Last year, it was Karur in Tamil Nadu and the Maha Kumbh in Prayagraj. The locations change, the crowds differ, but the tragedy keeps repeating itself.This raises an important question: despite elaborate planning and dedicated crowd management teams, why do stampedes keep happening? And what can authorities do to prevent a small disturbance from turning into a disaster?Public excitement soars during religious gatherings. Actual turnout often exceeds what authorities anticipate, resulting in more people entering an area than it can safely accommodate.As the crowd swells, even a small disturbance, a rumour, someone tripping and falling, a sudden power outage or even a broken barricade can lead to a situation in which people lose control of their movement.According to a 2014 report by the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), titled Managing Crowd at Events and Venues of Mass Gathering: A Guide for State Government, Local Authorities, Administrators and Organizers, crowd disasters can be triggered by several factors.Structural problems such as weak temporary structures, collapsed barricades, poorly lit stairways, slippery roads and narrow entrances and exits can lead to a crowd crush.Fires, electrical failures and security scares can also turn an otherwise manageable gathering into a dangerous crush.The report explains the causes of stampedes through the "FIST" model which is an acronym for Force, Information, Space and Time. According to the model, the four factors that can contribute to a crowd disaster are the force exerted by the crowd, the information that triggers its reaction, the physical space available and the duration of the incident."The FIST circumstances namely crowd force, the information upon which the crowd acts, the physical space involved, and the time duration of the incident play a very important role resulting in either overcrowding or high desired velocity," the report says.In simple terms, when too many people are packed into a limited space, pressure builds as those behind continue moving forward while those in front are unable to move. At extreme crowd densities, people can be pushed against one another with such force that they lose control of their movements. Even those who remain standing can struggle to breathe.Deaths in such situations do not necessarily occur because someone has literally been "trampled" under the feet of others. The NDMA says compressive asphyxia, which occurs when pressure on the chest prevents a person from breathing, has historically been the most common cause of death in crowd disasters."On occasions, this has led to deaths because of crushing, suffocation, and trampling. Historically, compressive asphyxia has been the most common reason for deaths in crowd disasters," the report says.Crowd psychology is also a factor that can contribute to a stampede-like situation. According to the NDMA report, individuals often conform their thoughts and behaviour to those of a larger group rather than acting independently."Individual behaviour in a crowd is sometimes influenced by the behaviour of others. The individuals within a crowd may act differently than if they were on their own," it says."The unlawful actions of a few people can result in larger numbers following them. Research has shown that understanding of crowd behaviour has led to community based approach to crowd control instead of force based control," the report adds.For instance, long queues at places of worship may lead some devotees to climb over fences, prompting others to follow and causing overcrowding in another area.However, crowd behaviour is not always irrational. People react to incomplete information, the movement of others and the fear of danger. In dense crowds, they may also lose the ability to control their own movement.This is why rumours and misleading announcements can be particularly dangerous. People may begin moving towards an exit without knowing what is happening elsewhere in the venue. If the exit is already congested, the sudden movement can increase pressure on those trapped in the crowd.Talking to The Times of India, former Bihar director general of police Abhayanand, who handled several such gatherings during his long service, said police should refrain from using force when a crowd is already panicked during a stampede-like situation."There is always a trigger, however small. It is followed immediately thereafter by a rumour which spreads like wildfire," Abhayanand said."I haven't followed any SOP in my days. I followed two basics: The crowd has panicked. Don't increase the panic by lathi charge. If there is an individual in whom the crowd has trust and if he can be made to communicate with the crowd, its effect is magical," he added."Crowds where there is some common binding force experience stampede. Such stampedes are easier to manage," he further said.Abhayanand also recalled handling a similar situation during the funeral procession of Ranvir Sena chief Brahmeshwar Mukhiya in Patna in 2012. He said police refrained from using force against a particularly unruly gathering of supporters."The crowd was itching for a trigger, and a police lathi charge could have set things off. We restrained ourselves because the repercussions would not have been limited to the capital but could have spread across the entire state," he told TOI."Those indulging in arson wanted the police to react and resort to a lathi charge. That was precisely what they were trying to provoke, but we did not allow that trigger to be pulled," he added.His account points to the importance of police response when a crowd is already on edge. An attempt to disperse people by force can worsen the situation if it causes them to rush towards a narrow exit or move against an incoming crowd.The NDMA has also laid down guidelines on how authorities should manage crowds and respond when a stampede-like situation develops.According to the agency, the guiding principle should be to bridge the gap between demand and supply. This requires controlling the number of people entering a venue, regulating the crowd within it and managing the outflow when necessary.The NDMA recommends designated staging points through which visitors should pass, along with effective systems to count and monitor people moving through them. Multiple routes should be encouraged to prevent bottlenecks and facilitate the movement of vulnerable groups.Crowd management also requires authorities to anticipate disturbances without allowing their response to trigger a larger crisis."Such miscreants should be immediately quarantined and removed. Action should be taken immediately with tact and firmness, without inviting undue attention from the general public, which may be there if force is used," it says."Inappropriate or poorly managed control procedures may precipitate crowd incidents rather than preventing them. For example, police reacting to a group of unruly people may chase them in a direction opposite to the incoming crowd, which may create a collision, and hence a disaster. Special attention should also be given to the border of the venue and the floating crowd moving there because the mischief is usually caused at such places," it adds.The agency also recommends "input control" by restricting or staggering entry to prevent overcrowding. Authorities must be able to regulate, slow or temporarily stop the inflow when a venue reaches its safe capacity.This also means keeping entry and exit routes clear, ensuring that people leaving a venue do not collide with those entering, and monitoring areas where crowds tend to gather or stop moving.Communication is another important part of crowd management. The NDMA says a lack of reliable information can cause people to panic or change direction, leading to dangerous crowd movements."Communicating with visitors and providing them with the correct information is a very critical factor in all situations," the report says, stressing that communication is essential during normal operations, emergencies and recovery.The Kolkata tragedy showed how quickly things can go wrong when these safeguards fail. Police said the crowd had become congested near the exit during the rain, even as the entry point remained open. The misleading announcement about the pandal collapsing is believed to have added to the pressure, although investigators are still examining the exact sequence of events.Ultimately, effective crowd management lies in anticipating pressure, regulating movement and ensuring that a small trigger does not turn into an uncontrollable chain of events. The challenge is not just to prepare for the thousands expected to attend an event, but also to recognise when a gathering is becoming unsafe and act before it is too late.
Article Summary: Stampede at Kolkata pandal during Durga Puja claimed 19 lives. India is a country of festivals, and its massive religious gatherings also make it prone to stampedes. Structural problems such as weak temporary structures, collapsed barricades, poorly lit stairways and narrow entrances and exits can lead to a crowd crush.

Article Title: 'Don't push us': SC warns of harsh stand on firecrackers if orders go unenforced

Article Title: From Hitler’s rise to farmers’ misery in India: How the Great Depression changed lives far beyond America
Article Text:
Germany’s economic collapse turned Hitler into a political force

India’s farmers were crushed as crop prices collapsed

Britain’s industrial decline pushed millions out of work

From Wall Street to the World

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

In October 1929, billions of dollars in wealth evaporated from the American stock market, setting off an economic catastrophe that would reach far beyond Wall Street.Years of speculative buying, easy credit and inflated share prices had created a market built on the expectation that stocks would keep rising. When confidence collapsed, investors rushed to sell. The Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged nearly 13 per cent on October 28 and another 12 per cent the following day, in what became known as Black Monday and Black Tuesday.But the crash was only the beginning. Bank failures, collapsing demand and business closures deepened the American downturn, while the withdrawal of US loans, falling international trade and the constraints of the gold standard carried the crisis across borders.The result was the Great Depression, a global disaster that would help propel Adolf Hitler towards power in Germany, devastate farmers in colonial India, push millions of Britons into unemployment, and expose the fragility of economies around the world.What followed was not merely a financial collapse, but a decade of economic hardship and political upheaval that changed the course of the twentieth century.The Great Depression hit Germany at a time when its economy was already vulnerable, turning a global financial crisis into a national catastrophe.The country was still struggling with the consequences of the First World War, including reparations, political instability and the devastating hyperinflation of 1923.Its recovery during the second half of the 1920s depended heavily on foreign credit, particularly loans from the United States.Under the Dawes Plan of 1924, American lending helped stabilise German finances and supported economic recovery. But this dependence became a major weakness when the Wall Street crash struck in October 1929.As American banks and investors came under pressure, new lending dried up and foreign creditors recalled short-term loans. German banks and businesses struggled to obtain credit, investment declined and companies began cutting production and jobs.The consequences were severe. Industrial output contracted, businesses failed and unemployment soared. By 1932, around 5.6 million Germans were registered as unemployed, while industrial production had fallen by approximately 40 per cent from its 1928 level.The crisis also paralysed political decision-making. Chancellor Hermann Müller’s coalition government collapsed in March 1930 amid disagreements over unemployment insurance, paving the way for increasingly unstable governments that relied on presidential emergency powers.This economic desperation created an opening for Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party. They portrayed the Weimar Republic as weak and incapable of protecting ordinary Germans, promising jobs, national revival and decisive leadership. Their message appealed to sections of the middle class, struggling farmers, small business owners and workers disillusioned with the political establishment.The electoral shift was dramatic. According to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, the Nazis won just 2.6 per cent of the vote in the 1928 parliamentary election. Their share rose to 18 per cent in September 1930 and 37 per cent in July 1932, making them the largest party in the Reichstag.Nazi campaigning deliberately exploited the hardship. A 1932 election poster preserved by the US Holocaust Memorial Museum carried the slogan “Our Last Hope - Hitler”, presenting the Nazi leader as an answer to national despair.The party used mass rallies, newspapers, posters and speeches to promise economic recovery and political order. At the same time, it spread antisemitic conspiracy theories, blamed Jews and communists for Germany’s problems, and attacked democratic institutions.Hitler did not win an outright majority in a free national election. On January 30, 1933, President Paul von Hindenburg appointed him chancellor following negotiations with conservative political leaders who believed they could control him. The Nazis subsequently dismantled democracy and established a dictatorship.The Great Depression did not, by itself, cause Hitler’s rise. But the collapse of American lending, mass unemployment and the failure of Germany’s political leadership to restore confidence created conditions that the Nazis exploited with devastating consequences.In British-ruled India, the Great Depression turned a global economic crisis into a rural emergency, exposing the financial vulnerability of millions of cultivators and deepening resentment against colonial rule.As international demand weakened and agricultural prices plunged, farmers earned less from their crops but continued to face debts, rent and land revenue obligations. For many, the crisis meant selling produce at a loss, struggling to repay moneylenders and risking the loss of their land.A 2022 research paper by historian Alok Oak, published in Studies in Indian Politics, documents the scale of the collapse. India’s agricultural price index fell from 203 in 1929 to 127 in 1931, using 1873 as the base year. The price index for raw cotton dropped from 133 to 70 over the same period. The decline was particularly damaging for cultivators who depended on commercial crops to generate cash for household expenses, rent and taxes.The crisis was compounded by the structure of the colonial economy. According to Oak, the British government refused to devalue the rupee amid concerns about meeting its foreign financial obligations. Meanwhile, Britain’s exports to India fell from £90.6 million in 1924 to £52.9 million in 1930, a decline of about 41 per cent. Falling trade and agricultural prices squeezed rural incomes and weakened economic activity.The timing was significant for India’s independence movement. At its Lahore session in December 1929, the Indian National Congress declared Purna Swaraj, or complete independence, as its goal. On January 26, 1930, Congress observed Independence Day, building momentum for a new phase of resistance.The Depression did not create the struggle against British rule, which had much deeper roots, but worsening economic conditions made questions of taxation, rural livelihoods and control over India’s economy more urgent.Mahatma Gandhi launched the Civil Disobedience Movement in 1930, beginning with the Salt March from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi. By challenging the British monopoly on salt and the tax imposed on a basic necessity, Gandhi chose an issue that affected Indians across social and economic divisions. The campaign transformed an everyday grievance into an act of mass resistance and helped bring the nationalist movement into the lives of ordinary people.Gandhi also urged Indians to boycott foreign goods, particularly British-made cloth, and promoted khadi and domestic production. These campaigns had a political and economic purpose. Reducing dependence on imported goods could challenge British commercial interests while encouraging Indians to support local producers. At a time when the global crisis had exposed the vulnerability of export-dependent economies, the message of economic self-reliance gained added significanceResearch by Stanford University political scientists Rikhil Bhavnani and Saumitra Jha has also identified a link between economic shocks and nationalist mobilisation. Their working paper found that districts producing export crops and affected by interwar trade shocks, including the Depression, were more likely to support the independence movement in the 1937 and 1946 elections.The researchers argue that these shocks helped bring agricultural exporters into a broader coalition demanding political change. The findings suggest that the Depression’s political consequences extended beyond immediate protests and influenced support for nationalism in subsequent years.The crisis also reinforced Gandhi’s emphasis on village industries and economic self-reliance. He argued that political freedom would mean little if rural India remained trapped in poverty and dependent on external markets. Gandhi promoted khadi and cottage industries as ways to create employment, strengthen village economies and reduce dependence on imported goods.In 1934, the All-India Village Industries Association was established to advance this wider effort. Historian Alok Oak argues that the Depression and the limits of colonial economic policy helped strengthen Gandhi’s focus on rural production and economic autonomy.Britain entered the Great Depression with its traditional industries already struggling to compete in international markets. Coal mining, shipbuilding, iron and textiles faced declining demand and growing competition, leaving industrial communities vulnerable when the Wall Street crash of 1929 further restricted global trade.As exports weakened and businesses cut production, unemployment soared. According to the UK National Archives, the number of unemployed people climbed to almost 3.5 million by 1932, with the North East of England, Scotland’s industrial lowlands and the mining valleys of Wales among the hardest-hit regions.Families faced prolonged hardship, while the government’s introduction of a means test in 1931 intensified resentment among people seeking unemployment assistance.The crisis also exposed the limits of Britain’s monetary policy. The country had returned to the gold standard in 1925, tying sterling to a fixed gold value. As economic activity contracted, deflation deepened and unemployment rose, the government faced growing pressure to defend the pound while supporting the domestic economy.The situation became critical in 1931 as investors withdrew funds from London and the Bank of England lost gold reserves. The National Archives’ record of the government’s September 20 announcement says more than £200 million had been withdrawn from the London market since mid-July. Britain suspended the gold standard the following day.The political consequences were immediate. The Labour government under Ramsay MacDonald split over how to address the financial emergency and public spending. MacDonald subsequently formed a National Government with Conservative and Liberal support, while Labour suffered a major defeat in the October 1931 election.The departure from gold eventually gave Britain greater freedom to lower interest rates and allowed sterling to depreciate, helping exporters and supporting the early stages of recovery.A research paper by economists Jason Lennard and Meredith M Paker found that leaving the gold standard reduced unemployment by 2.7 percentage points in export-intensive industries relative to less export-dependent industries.Yet recovery was uneven. Traditional industrial regions continued to experience hardship, and hunger marches brought the plight of unemployed workers into public view.Britain’s experience demonstrated how the Great Depression could undermine established industries, destabilise governments and force a major economic power to abandon a monetary system it had once considered essential to financial stability.The Great Depression proved that an economic crisis does not stop at a country’s borders. A stock market collapse in America helped fuel the rise of Hitler in Germany, deepened the misery of farmers in colonial India, pushed millions of Britons out of work, and devastated economies around the world.Yet the damage went far beyond lost jobs, failed banks and falling crop prices. Across continents, the Depression changed not only how people earned a living, but also how they viewed their governments and their future.Its legacy helped reshape the global economic order. The failure of protectionism, the instability of international finance and the inability of countries to contain the crisis through isolated national responses influenced the push for greater economic cooperation after the Second World War, including the Bretton Woods system.But the Depression’s most enduring warning is political as much as economic: when livelihoods collapse and governments appear powerless, public anger can become an opening for extremism.The crash began on Wall Street in 1929; its consequences reached farms, factories, homes and parliaments around the world, changing the course of the twentieth century.
Article Summary: The Great Depression hit Germany at a time when its economy was already vulnerable, turning a global financial crisis into a national catastrophe. The country was still struggling with the consequences of the First World War, including reparations, political instability and the devastating hyperinflation of 1923. The economic desperation created an opening for Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party.

Article Title: India calls for protecting freedom of navigation, global trade at UN amid maritime security threats

India on Thursday strongly condemned attacks against commercial vessels, advocating freedom of navigation and unimpeded maritime commerce at the United Nations India' permanent Representative to the United Nations, Harish Parvathaneni, stressed the need to protect seafarers in accordance with international law.Speaking at the UN Security Council's open debate on emerging technologies and maritime security on Thursday, Parvathaneni said disruptions at critical maritime choke points could have consequences far beyond their immediate geographical locations.“Recent attacks against commercial shipping have demonstrated how disruptions at critical maritime choke points can have consequences far beyond their immediate geography,” he said, adding that such incidents threaten seafarers, disrupt supply chains and disproportionately affect developing countries through higher costs and economic uncertainty.Parvathaneni also highlighted the growing role of emerging technologies in maritime security, noting that artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, satellite-based surveillance and advanced cyber capabilities offered opportunities to strengthen security but could also infrastructure to cyber threats.The proliferation of autonomous systems, he said, raised complex questions relating to attribution, accountability and unintended escalation. He called for appropriate safeguards, meaningful human oversight and clear responsibility in the deployment of emerging technologies.He said the UN Charter and international law, including the law of the sea as reflected in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos), provided the essential framework for state conduct.The Security Council, he added, should focus on technological developments with demonstrable implications for international peace and security, while encouraging practical cooperation, confidence-building and resilience.Parvathaneni said India had identified artificial intelligence and maritime security as important priorities for its candidature to the Security Council for 2028–2029.“Our objective is clear: technology must strengthen human security, not undermine it; it must expand opportunity, not inequality; and it must make our shared maritime commons safer, not more contested,” he said.

Article Title: Poverty plunges in India, but top 10% earn 13 times more than bottom 10%: World Bank
Article Text:
Amid heaps of trash, countless underprivileged children in India sort waste to earn a meager living, an invisible workforce fueling the country’s recycling economy.

Sharp decline in poverty

Rural poverty remains higher

More jobs, but wages remain stagnant

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is the biggest barrier to reducing poverty in rural parts of India? Lack of quality employment opportunities Limited educational access Insufficient government support 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: India has lifted an estimated 496 million people out of poverty between 2011 and 2023, recording one of the world's fastest declines in poverty over the period. However, significant income inequality persists, with workers in the country's top 10% earning a median income nearly 13 times higher than those in the bottom 10%, according to the World Bank's October 2026 India Poverty and Equity Brief.The report highlights India's progress in reducing both extreme and multidimensional poverty but flags persistent challenges such as stagnant real wages, poor employment quality and unequal access to economic opportunities.The share of India's population living below the lower-middle-income poverty line of $4.20 a day, measured at 2021 purchasing power parity (PPP), fell sharply from 57.7% in 2011 to 16.1% in 2023.Extreme poverty also witnessed a significant decline. The proportion of people living on less than $3 a day dropped from 27.1% to 2.6% during the same period.Despite the overall progress, poverty remains unevenly distributed across the country. Rural poverty stood at 19.3% in 2023, significantly higher than the 8.6% recorded in urban areas, based on the $4.20-a-day threshold.The report noted that households with lower educational attainment, fewer assets, limited access to stable employment and higher dependency ratios remain particularly vulnerable.Geographically, states across a contiguous belt stretching from Uttar Pradesh to West Bengal accounted for around 57% of India's poor population.The World Bank said further poverty reduction would increasingly depend on creating more productive employment opportunities in these regions, particularly through better-quality non-farm jobs.India added around 134 million employed people between 2017 and 2023, nearly twice the increase in its working-age population. A significant share of this growth came from rural women entering paid employment, increasing the number of earning members in households.However, the rise in employment has not translated into comparable wage growth. The report noted that real earnings remained broadly unchanged, with much of the employment expansion concentrated in relatively low-productivity activities.It also flagged limitations in measuring inequality, noting that improvements in recent household surveys may account for part of the reported welfare gains, while wealthier households may not be fully represented, potentially leading to an underestimation of inequality.
Article Summary: India has lifted an estimated 496 million people out of poverty between 2011 and 2023. However, significant income inequality persists, with workers in the country's top 10% earning a median income nearly 13 times higher than those in the bottom 10%. Rural poverty stood at 19.3% in 2023, significantly higher than the 8.6% recorded in urban areas.

Article Title: Glacial lake outburst in Bhutan: North Bengal on red alert as flood threat looms; thousands evacuated
Article Text:
A major Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) occurred on Thursday evening, October 29, 2026, at Shintaphu Lake (also known as Lemthang or Shintaphu Tsho) in the Gasa district of northwestern Bhutan.

West Bengal shifts thousands to safety

Assam monitors possible impact in Dhubri

What is a glacial lake outburst flood?
